title: MedMisBench: Measuring Epistemic Resilience of LLMs Under Misleading Medical Context
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: A single plausible-sounding authoritative false statement injected into a question can flip a model's correct answer to a targeted wrong one.
layout: Stacked top-to-bottom flow, question and choices on top, injection and responses below, color-highlighted spans
description: A worked example of the failure mode, read top to bottom. At the top left is a MedMisBench question about melanoma excision margins. At the top right are answer choices A–E: the correct D is highlighted green with a check mark, and the targeted wrong B is highlighted red with a warning icon. Below them, an AI robot icon points to a dashed box, 'Pre-Injection Response (Correct)', with green highlights on the right reasoning and Answer D. Next, a yellow 'Injection Sentence' box carries a syringe icon, an 'Authority' provenance icon and a fabricated hospital-SOP threshold claim. Red highlights mark the misleading parts. An arrow leads to a second robot labelled 'Easily Mislead!' and a dashed 'Post-Injection Response (Incorrect)' box. That box repeats the false threshold in yellow, and the wrong Answer B appears in red.
caption: Focused false context can redirect a correct medical judgment. An authority-framed threshold/reference claim moves the model from the correct melanoma-management answer to the targeted wrong option.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now reach expert-level scores on medical licensing exams, encouraging the assumption that high scores imply safe medical judgment while patients increasingly use them for health advice. We show this assumption is fragile: when misleading context is injected into questions that LLMs originally answer correctly, they abandon the correct answer. We call the ability to maintain correct judgment under adversarial context epistemic resilience, and introduce MedMisBench to measure it. MedMisBench contains 10,932 medical question items and 48,889 misleading context-option pairs spanning medical reasoning, agentic capability, and patient-journey evaluation. Across 11 model configurations, mean accuracy falls from 71.1% on original questions to 38.0% under focused misleading context, with 51.5% attack success. The most damaging injections are formal, rule-like fabrications: authority-framed falsehoods reach 69.5% attack success and exception-poisoning claims reach 64.1%. A 14-member clinical panel from 7 countries identified serious potential harm in 38.2% of reviewed cases. MedMisBench exposes a structural blind spot in LLM evaluation in medical settings: existing benchmarks measure what models know, but not whether they preserve correct medical judgment under misleading context.
